explanations.explanation: Governor it is, friend. Nebuchadnezzar appointed Gedaliah over the people he left behind, and the commanders hear that Gedaliah has the job. A governor runs things for the king, and that's the seat Gedaliah sits in here.

Prophet is a title you hear a lot in the Bible, but it's not this one. The passage never calls Gedaliah that. The text says the king of Babylon appointed him over the people left behind in Judah, and the commanders hear he is governor.

Nope, no priest here. The text never gives Gedaliah that title, and it says the king of Babylon appointed him. The word that fits is governor. Mixing those up is like asking me to stamp cookies with a rolling pin: right kitchen, wrong tool.

Ishmael son of Nethaniah is on the list, right along with Johanan, Seraiah and Jaazaniah. All four come to Gedaliah at Mizpah with their men. Keep his name handy, because you'll hear it again in this passage.

Joab son of Zeruiah was David's army commander (2 Samuel 8:16), so I see why he came to mind. But he isn't one of the four named here. The commanders who come to Gedaliah are Ishmael, Johanan, Seraiah and Jaazaniah. Joab's story belongs to a much earlier day.

Abner son of Ner was the commander of Saul's army (1 Samuel 14:50), so he's a real army name. He just isn't in this passage. The four commanders are Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth and Jaazaniah. Nice try pulling a name from the Bible's army roster, though.
That's the line. Gedaliah says, “Do not be afraid of the servants of the Chaldeans.” He says it as an oath, before the commanders and their men.

The oath doesn't mention prophets at all. What Gedaliah says is, “Do not be afraid of the servants of the Chaldeans.” The fear on the table here is about the Chaldeans, not about anybody in Jerusalem.

Egypt doesn't come up in Gedaliah's oath. He says, “Do not be afraid of the servants of the Chaldeans.” Egypt does show up later in this passage, but as a place people run to, not a thing he tells them not to fear.

explanations.answer: It will be well with them
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. Gedaliah says, “Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you.” That's the whole promise, plain and simple. He gives no timeline and adds no extras.

That promise isn't in the oath. Gedaliah tells them to live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and then says, “…and it will be well with you.” Ruling Jerusalem again never comes up. I know it's a big hope to attach to a promise, but the text keeps it smaller.
Gedaliah doesn't say that. His oath ends with “…and it will be well with you.” Families coming home isn't part of what he promises here, and the passage doesn't add it.

True, friend. The text says all the people, small and great, together with the commanders of the army, arose and fled to Egypt. Everybody is on the move at once. It's a heavy moment, and the passage doesn't soften it.

Actually, it's true. The text says all the people, small and great, together with the commanders of the army, arose and fled to Egypt. The commanders go along with the crowd. That was a heavy day, so I'll just say it plainly.

explanations.answer: They are afraid of the Chaldeans
explanations.explanation: That's what the text gives. They fled to Egypt “…for fear of the Chaldeans.” The people small and great and the commanders of the army all arose and fled. Fear is the reason the verse names, and it doesn't say anything beyond that.

explanations.answer: They are following the king of Egypt
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a king of Egypt in this scene. It says the people and the commanders fled to Egypt “…for fear of the Chaldeans.” Fear is the reason the verse gives, so that's the reason I go with.

explanations.answer: They are running from a famine
explanations.explanation: No famine is mentioned in these verses. The text says they fled “…for fear of the Chaldeans.” Fear is the reason the verse gives, so that's the reason I give too.

Released, friend. Evil-merodach, the new king of Babylon, let King Jehoiachin out of prison in the year he became king. The text dates it to the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's exile. Prison door open, just like that.

explanations.answer: He sends him back to Judah
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't send him home. Evil-merodach releases Jehoiachin from prison, and the other kings with him are in Babylon too. So Jehoiachin is free, but the passage keeps him in Babylon.

No, the story goes the opposite way. Evil-merodach, Babylon's new king, releases King Jehoiachin from prison. Jehoiachin goes from a cell to a kind word from the king. Good news after a long stretch of hard news.

Other way around, friend. The text says Evil-merodach set Jehoiachin's throne above the thrones of the other kings who were with him in Babylon. Jehoiachin gets the higher seat, not the lower one. That's a big upgrade from where he started the story.

False is right, friend. The text says the king spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and set his throne above the thrones of the other kings who were with him in Babylon. Above, not below. I once got moved to the back of a junk drawer. Jehoiachin got moved UP.
It's bigger than a one-time honor. The text says Jehoiachin dined regularly at the king's table for the rest of his life. Regularly, friend. That's a standing seat, not a single dinner invitation.

False it is, friend. Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes and dined regularly at the king's table for the rest of his life. Prison clothes off, regular seat at the table. I'd have changed so fast my hat would've stayed behind.

explanations.answer: For the rest of his life
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. The king provided Jehoiachin a daily portion for the rest of his life. It's every single day, with no end date written in. A good way to close out the passage.
The text doesn't tie the portion to going home. It says the king provided a daily portion for the rest of his life. No condition and no countdown, just the rest of his life.

The text doesn't put a one-year limit on it. The king provided Jehoiachin a daily portion for the rest of his life. A year would've been nice, but the verse doesn't count in years. It counts in a whole life.
